Below I separate `supported fact` from `inference`, `uncertainty`, `disagreement`, and `lack of good evidence`.

**Supported Fact**

User-agent groups:
A robots.txt `group` is one or more `user-agent` lines followed by one or more rules; the group ends at the next `user-agent` line or end of file, and the last group may have no rules, which implicitly allows everything. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

A crawler uses its product token to find relevant groups. The product token must contain only letters, underscores, and hyphens, and crawlers must use case-insensitive matching to find the group that matches the product token. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

If more than one group matches the user-agent, the crawler must combine those groups’ rules into one group and then parse that combined group under the rule-processing rules in Section 2.2.2. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

If no matching group exists, crawlers must obey the group whose `user-agent` value is `*`, if such a group is present. If no group matches and there is no `*` group, or if no groups are present at all, then no rules apply. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

Allow/disallow precedence:
To decide whether a URI is allowed, a crawler must match the URI against the paths in `allow` and `disallow` rules. Matching should be case-sensitive, must start with the first octet of the path, and the most specific match must be used. RFC 9309 defines the “most specific” match as the one with the most octets. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

If an `allow` rule and a `disallow` rule are equivalent, the `allow` rule should be used. If no rule in the applicable group matches, or if the group has no rules, the URI is allowed. The `/robots.txt` URI is implicitly allowed. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

Percent encoding:
Before comparison, octets in the URI and in robots.txt paths that are outside ASCII, and octets in the reserved range defined by RFC 3986, must be percent-encoded. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

If the URI contains a percent-encoded ASCII octet, it must be decoded before comparison, unless the octet is a reserved URI character under RFC 3986 or is outside the unreserved range. The match is positive only if the rule path ends before any octet difference is encountered. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

RFC 9309 also says crawlers must support special characters such as `*` and `$`, and if crawlers need to match those characters literally in the URI, they should use percent encoding. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

Unavailable robots.txt responses:
RFC 9309 defines `Unavailable` as the case where the crawler tries to fetch `/robots.txt` and the server responds with a status indicating the resource is unavailable; in HTTP, 4xx status codes are given as the example. If the status indicates the robots.txt file is unavailable to the crawler, the crawler may access any resources on the server. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

By contrast, if robots.txt is `Unreachable` because of server or network errors, the file is considered undefined and the crawler must assume complete disallow; in HTTP, 5xx status codes are given as the example. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

**Inference**

A practical summary of RFC 9309 is: first determine the applicable user-agent group(s), merge them if multiple groups match, then resolve `allow` versus `disallow` by longest-path match, with `allow` winning ties, after doing the RFC’s required percent-encoding normalization. This is a synthesis of multiple normative statements in the RFC, not a single sentence stated verbatim there. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

**Uncertainty**

RFC 9309 says 4xx codes are an example of `Unavailable`, not an exhaustive enumeration in the text I reviewed, so I can support “4xx are included as an example,” but I would not overclaim a complete per-status-code matrix from this source alone. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

**Disagreement**

I found no disagreement in the primary source itself about these four points. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

**Lack of Good Evidence**

I do not have good evidence from RFC 9309 alone for crawler-specific behavior beyond the RFC’s requirements and examples, such as how every real crawler handles borderline user-agent matching cases or every unusual HTTP status. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

# RFC 9309 Robots Exclusion Protocol - Key Sections

## No Matching Group Behavior

"If no matching group exists, crawlers MUST obey the group with a user-agent line with the "*" value, if present." Additionally, "If no group matches the product token and there is no group with a user-agent line with the "*" value, or no groups are present at all, no rules apply."

## Allow and Disallow Rules

The specification requires that "a crawler MUST match the paths in "allow" and "disallow" rules against the URI." Critically, "The most specific match found MUST be used. The most specific match is the match that has the most octets."

For encoding: "Octets in the URI and robots.txt paths outside the range of the ASCII coded character set...MUST be percent-encoded as defined by [RFC3986] prior to comparison."

The document clarifies that "If no match is found amongst the rules in a group for a matching user-agent or there are no rules in the group, the URI is allowed. The /robots.txt URI is implicitly allowed."

## Access Results

**Successful Access:** "If the crawler successfully downloads the robots.txt file, the crawler MUST follow the parseable rules."

**Redirects:** Crawlers "SHOULD follow at least five consecutive redirects." Beyond five redirects, "crawlers MAY assume that the robots.txt file is unavailable."

**Unavailable Status:** When a server responds with 400-499 status codes, "the crawler MAY access any resources on the server."

**Unreachable Status:** On 500-599 errors, "the crawler MUST assume complete disallow."

## Caching Rules

"Crawlers MAY cache the fetched robots.txt file's contents...Crawlers SHOULD NOT use the cached version for more than 24 hours, unless the robots.txt file is unreachable."

## (a) Table from Section 2.2.2

| Path | Encoded Path | Path to Match |
|------|--------------|---------------|
| /foo/bar?baz=quz | /foo/bar?baz=quz | /foo/bar?baz=quz |
| /foo/bar?baz=https://foo.bar | /foo/bar?baz=https%3A%2F%2Ffoo.bar | /foo/bar?baz=https%3A%2F%2Ffoo.bar |
| /foo/bar/U+E38384 | /foo/bar/%E3%83%84 | /foo/bar/%E3%83%84 |

## (b) Special Characters Table and Example

| Character | Description | Example |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| # | Designates a line comment | allow: / # comment in line |
| $ | Designates the end of the match pattern | allow: /this/path/exactly$ |
| * | Designates 0 or more instances of any character | allow: /this/*/exactly |

Example robots.txt snippet:
```
allow: /this/path/exactly$
allow: /this/*/exactly
```

## (c) Section 2.3.1.3 "Unavailable" Status

"'Unavailable' means the crawler tries to fetch the robots.txt file and the server responds with status codes indicating that the resource in question is unavailable. For example, in the context of HTTP, such status codes are in the 400-499 range.

If a server status code indicates that the robots.txt file is unavailable to the crawler, then the crawler MAY access any resources on the server."

## (d) Section 2.3.1.5 "Parsing Errors"

"Crawlers MUST try to parse each line of the robots.txt file. Crawlers MUST use the parseable rules."

## (e) ABNF and Merge Example

**ABNF for group/rule lines:**
```
group = startgroupline
        *(startgroupline / emptyline)
        *(rule / emptyline)

startgroupline = *WS "user-agent" *WS ":" *WS product-token EOL

rule = *WS ("allow" / "disallow") *WS ":"
       *WS (path-pattern / empty-pattern) EOL
```

# "Unreachable" Status Subsection

"If the robots.txt file is unreachable due to server or network errors, this means the robots.txt file is undefined and the crawler MUST assume complete disallow. For example, in the context of HTTP, server errors are identified by status codes in the 500-599 range.

If the robots.txt file is undefined for a reasonably long period of time (for example, 30 days), crawlers MAY assume that the robots.txt file is unavailable as defined in Section 2.3.1.3 or continue to use a cached copy."

---

# Redirects Subsection

"It's possible that a server responds to a robots.txt fetch request with a redirect, such as HTTP 301 or HTTP 302 in the case of HTTP. The crawlers SHOULD follow at least five consecutive redirects, even across authorities (for example, hosts in the case of HTTP).

If a robots.txt file is reached within five consecutive redirects, the robots.txt file MUST be fetched, parsed, and its rules followed in the context of the initial authority.

If there are more than five consecutive redirects, crawlers MAY assume that the robots.txt file is unavailable."

## RFC 9309 (Robots Exclusion Protocol, September 2022)

All quotes below come from the RFC text at [rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt) / [datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9309](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9309) (same document, two renderings). I retrieved the text through a page-fetching tool that summarizes; passages in quotation marks were returned as verbatim extractions and were consistent across at least two independent fetches unless I flag otherwise.

---

### 1. User-agent groups (Section 2.2.1)

**Supported facts:**

- A crawler identifies itself with a **product token** containing "only uppercase and lowercase letters ("a-z" and "A-Z"), underscores ("_"), and hyphens ("-")", and the token "SHOULD be a substring of the identification string that the crawler sends" (e.g. its User-Agent header). ([rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt))
- Matching of the product token against `user-agent:` lines is **case-insensitive**: crawlers "apply case-insensitive matching to find the group that matches the product token and then obey the rules of the group." ([rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt))
- **Multiple groups with the same token merge:** "If more than one group matches the product token, the matching groups' rules MUST be combined into one group and parsed according to Section 2.2.2." The RFC gives an example where two `user-agent: ExampleBot` groups with `disallow: /foo`, `disallow: /bar` and `disallow: /baz` become a single group carrying all three rules. ([datatracker rendering](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html))
- **Fallback:** "If no matching group exists, crawlers MUST obey the group with a user-agent line with the "*" value, if present." ([rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt))
- **No group at all:** "If no group matches the product token and there is no group with a user-agent line with the "*" value, or no groups are present at all, no rules apply." ([rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt)) — i.e. everything is crawlable.
- ABNF: a group is one or more `startgroupline`s followed by rules, so consecutive `user-agent:` lines share the rule block that follows them:
  ```
  group = startgroupline *(startgroupline / emptyline) *(rule / emptyline)
  startgroupline = *WS "user-agent" *WS ":" *WS product-token EOL
  rule = *WS ("allow" / "disallow") *WS ":" *WS (path-pattern / empty-pattern) EOL
  ```
  ([rfc9309.html](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html))

**Uncertainty:** my first extraction of the fallback sentence rendered it as "*should* obey the group with `*`"; two later fetches returned **MUST**. I am treating MUST as correct (two-of-three agreement), but if the exact normative keyword matters to you, verify that single sentence directly in [Section 2.2.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9309#section-2.2.1).

---

### 2. Allow/disallow precedence (Section 2.2.2)

**Supported facts:**

- "A crawler MUST match the paths in "allow" and "disallow" rules against the URI." ([rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt))
- "The matching SHOULD be case sensitive. The matching MUST start with the first octet of the path." (prefix matching, not substring matching) ([rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt))
- **The precedence rule:** "The most specific match found MUST be used. The most specific match is the match that has the most octets." ([rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt)) — note this is length-based, not order-based, and `allow` does not automatically outrank `disallow`.
- **Default is allow:** "If no match is found amongst the rules in a group for a matching user-agent or there are no rules in the group, the URI is allowed. The /robots.txt URI is implicitly allowed." ([rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt))
- Special characters in patterns (Section 2.2.3): `#` = line comment; `$` = end of match pattern; `*` = 0 or more instances of any character. Examples given: `allow: / # comment in line`, `allow: /this/path/exactly$`, `allow: /this/*/exactly`. ([rfc9309.html](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html))

**Gap / inference (moderate confidence):** the text I retrieved contains **no tie-break rule** for the case where an `allow` and a `disallow` match with an identical number of octets. Google's open-source parser resolves such ties in favour of `allow`, but that is implementation behaviour, not something I verified in RFC 9309 itself — treat "allow wins ties" as *not* an RFC 9309 requirement unless you confirm it independently.

### 3. Percent encoding (Section 2.2.2, plus 2.2.3)

**Supported facts:**

- "Octets in the URI and robots.txt paths outside the range of the ASCII coded character set ... MUST be percent-encoded as defined by [RFC3986] prior to comparison." ([rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt))
- "If a percent-encoded ASCII octet is encountered in the URI, it MUST be unencoded prior to comparison, unless it is a reserved character in the URI as defined by [RFC3986] or the character is outside the unreserved character range." ([rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt); the trailing clause comes from the first fetch and matched the shorter renderings)
- Normalisation examples given in the RFC's table (columns *Path* / *Encoded Path* / *Path to Match*) ([rfc9309.html](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html)):

| Path | Encoded Path | Path to Match |
|---|---|---|
| `/foo/bar?baz=quz` | `/foo/bar?baz=quz` | `/foo/bar?baz=quz` |
| `/foo/bar?baz=https://foo.bar` | `/foo/bar?baz=https%3A%2F%2Ffoo.bar` | `/foo/bar?baz=https%3A%2F%2Ffoo.bar` |
| `/foo/bar/U+E38384` | `/foo/bar/%E3%83%84` | `/foo/bar/%E3%83%84` |
| `/foo/bar/%E3%83%84` | `/foo/bar/%E3%83%84` | `/foo/bar/%E3%83%84` |
| `/foo/bar/%62%61%7A` | `/foo/bar/%62%61%7A` | `/foo/bar/baz` |

  The last row is the key one: `%62%61%7A` are unreserved ASCII octets, so they decode to `baz` before comparison; reserved characters like `%3A` and `%2F` stay encoded.
- To match `#`, `$` or `*` **literally** rather than as pattern syntax: "If crawlers match special characters verbatim in the URI, crawlers SHOULD use "%" encoding." ([rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt))

**Known error in the published text:** the third table row's `U+E38384` is wrong; it is the subject of **Errata ID 7128**, which says it should read `U+30C4` (the character ツ, whose UTF-8 encoding is E3 83 84). Status: **Reported** (not yet verified by the responsible AD). ([errata.rfc-editor.org/rfc9309](https://errata.rfc-editor.org/rfc9309))

### 4. Unavailable / unreachable robots.txt (Section 2.3.1)

The RFC splits access results into five subsections — 2.3.1.1 Successful Access, 2.3.1.2 Redirects, 2.3.1.3 "Unavailable" Status, 2.3.1.4 "Unreachable" Status, 2.3.1.5 Parsing Errors ([datatracker ToC](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9309)).

**Supported facts:**

- **Successful access (2.3.1.1):** "If the crawler successfully downloads the robots.txt file, the crawler MUST follow the parseable rules." ([rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt))
- **Redirects (2.3.1.2):** "The crawlers SHOULD follow at least five consecutive redirects, even across authorities (for example, hosts in the case of HTTP). If a robots.txt file is reached within five consecutive redirects, the robots.txt file MUST be fetched, parsed, and its rules followed in the context of the initial authority. If there are more than five consecutive redirects, crawlers MAY assume that the robots.txt file is unavailable." ([datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9309))
- **"Unavailable" (2.3.1.3) — the 4xx case:** "'Unavailable' means the crawler tries to fetch the robots.txt file and the server responds with status codes indicating that the resource in question is unavailable. For example, in the context of HTTP, such status codes are in the 400-499 range. If a server status code indicates that the robots.txt file is unavailable to the crawler, then **the crawler MAY access any resources on the server**." ([rfc9309.html](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html)) — a 404 therefore means "crawl everything", and note 401/403 fall in the same bucket.
- **"Unreachable" (2.3.1.4) — the 5xx / network-error case:** "If the robots.txt file is unreachable due to server or network errors, this means the robots.txt file is undefined and **the crawler MUST assume complete disallow**. For example, in the context of HTTP, server errors are identified by status codes in the 500-599 range. If the robots.txt file is undefined for a reasonably long period of time (for example, 30 days), crawlers MAY assume that the robots.txt file is unavailable as defined in Section 2.3.1.3 or continue to use a cached copy." ([datatracker](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9309))
- **Parsing errors (2.3.1.5):** "Crawlers MUST try to parse each line of the robots.txt file. Crawlers MUST use the parseable rules." — unparseable lines are skipped, not treated as a fetch failure. ([rfc9309.html](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html))
- **Caching (2.4):** "Crawlers MAY cache the fetched robots.txt file's contents ... Crawlers SHOULD NOT use the cached version for more than 24 hours, unless the robots.txt file is unreachable." ([rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt))
- **Size limit (2.5):** "The parsing limit MUST be at least 500 kibibytes [KiB]." ([rfc9309.txt](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.txt))

**The asymmetry is the practical takeaway (inference, but a direct reading):** 4xx ⇒ open season; 5xx/network failure ⇒ full stop, degrading to "unavailable" only after a long outage (~30 days suggested) or falling back to cache.

### 5. Errata status

Four errata are currently listed for RFC 9309, **all with status "Reported"** — i.e. none has been verified, so the published RFC text stands as normative ([errata.rfc-editor.org/rfc9309](https://errata.rfc-editor.org/rfc9309)):

| ID | Section | Substance |
|---|---|---|
| 7124 | 5.2 | `disallow.gif` should be `disallowed.gif` in the example |
| 7128 | 2.2.2 | `U+E38384` should be `U+30C4` |
| 7995 | 2.2 | `path-pattern` ABNF should permit `*` as the first character — `("/" / "*") *UTF8-char-noctl` — to match the examples in Section 5.1 |
| 8895 | 2.3.1.5 | Proposes optional support for comma-separated user-agent tokens in one field |

Erratum 7995 is worth noting for implementers: as published, the ABNF appears to require patterns to start with `/`, while the RFC's own examples use leading `*`. That is a *reported* inconsistency, not a settled correction.

- The full verbatim text of Section 5 (the worked examples of group merging and of most-specific-match precedence) — I read the Section 2 normative text only.
- Whether any implementation-level consensus (Google, Bing, Common Crawl) diverges from the RFC on tie-breaking, `sitemap:`/`crawl-delay:` handling, or the 500 KiB limit. RFC 9309 is a Proposed Standard describing widely deployed practice, but conformance of any particular crawler is a separate empirical question I did not investigate here.
